\section{Linearity of the first mode in drive amplitude}
\label{app:lin}

Section~4.1.5 reports that the swept-sine replicates show no detected dependence
of $f_1$ on excitation level, and states a resolution of roughly 3.6\%. Both the
test and that resolution figure are set out here, because the resolution is what
the argument in Section~4.3 rests on rather than the $p$-value.

\subsection*{Captures}

Three drive amplitudes were recorded, three replicate sweeps at each, nine
captures in total. Amplitude is reported as the AC RMS of the response, which is
the available proxy for how hard the frame was driven. The ratio of the highest
to the lowest group mean is $2.22$, the factor of 2.2 quoted in Section~4.1.5.

\centering

replicates. Extraction is the project's standard peak-picking over the full band,
$0.5$ to $450$~Hz.}
\label{tab:lin-percapture}
\begin{tabular}{llrr}
\toprule
Gain & Replicate & AC RMS (g) & $f_1$ (Hz) \\
\midrule
1v4 & r1 & 0.32234 & 2.882 \\
1v4 & r2 & 0.32420 & 2.819 \\
1v4 & r3 & 0.32995 & 2.950 \\
\midrule

\midrule

Note that the drive level is nearly constant within a gain group, spanning at
most $3\%$, while $f_1$ varies by up to $0.13$~Hz within the same group. The
within-group variation is not a drive effect.

\subsection*{Tests}

Three statistics are reported on the same nine captures. They are not
alternative versions of one test: each uses a different subset of the data, and
the relationship between them is the point of this subsection.

\paragraph{The statistic quoted in Section~4.1.5.} Welch's two-sample $t$-test
comparing the \emph{extreme gains only}, 1v4 against 2v8, three replicates each:
$t = -0.63$, $\mathrm{df} = 3.21$, $p = 0.573$. This is the test the body cites.
It uses six of the nine captures and discards the middle gain entirely.

\paragraph{The same trend over all nine captures.} A linear regression of $f_1$
on drive RMS across every capture gives a slope of $-0.120$~Hz per unit RMS,
standard error $0.183$, $t = -0.66$ on 7 degrees of freedom, $p = 0.533$,
$r = -0.24$. This tests the same hypothesis as the first statistic, that $f_1$
trends with drive, but uses all the data and gains four degrees of freedom by
doing so. It agrees: no trend.

\paragraph{What the first two both miss.} A one-way analysis of variance across
the three gains gives $F(2,6) = 8.24$, $p = 0.019$. The group means differ
significantly, and neither test above can see it. The extreme-gain comparison
cannot, because the 1v4 and 2v8 means differ by only $0.028$~Hz while the
discarded 2v2 mean sits $0.147$~Hz above their midpoint: the omitted group is the
deviating one. The regression cannot, because the displacement is not ordered by
drive, so a straight line through it has near-zero slope.

Taken together: all three agree that $f_1$ carries no monotone trend with drive,
and the third shows that the swept-sine estimate nonetheless varies between
groups by more than its within-group scatter. That is a property of the estimator
and not of the structure, since the drive level within a gain group is nearly
constant while $f_1$ is not. Of the three, the statistic the body quotes is the
weakest: it uses the fewest captures and is the only one blind to the deviating
group. It is reported here alongside the other two so that the figure in
Section~4.1.5 can be located exactly and its basis is not ambiguous.

\subsection*{Resolution}

The pooled within-gain standard deviation is $0.0518$~Hz on 6 degrees of freedom.
Against the lowest-gain mean of $2.8836$~Hz that is $1.79\%$ of $f_1$, and twice
it is $3.59\%$, the figure quoted in Section~4.1.5 and in the assumptions table.
The derivation is therefore
%
\begin{equation*}
  \text{resolution} \;=\; \frac{2\,s_{\text{pooled}}}{\bar{f}_{1,\text{lowest gain}}}
  \;=\; \frac{2 \times 0.0518}{2.8836} \;=\; 3.59\%,
\end{equation*}
%
a two-standard-deviation figure, normalised by the lowest-gain group mean.

Two standard deviations is a rule of thumb rather than a formal detection limit.
The minimum difference this design could detect in a two-sample comparison at
three replicates per group, $\alpha = 0.05$ and $80\%$ power, is $0.153$~Hz, or
$5.30\%$ of $f_1$.

The formal threshold is therefore \emph{above} the two-sigma figure, so the test
is less sensitive than $3.59\%$ suggests. This strengthens the argument the
figure is used to make. Section~4.3 invokes the resolution to establish that this
test cannot license the trace-grade shifts, which run from $0.97\%$ to $2.29\%$;
a true threshold of $5.30\%$ places those shifts further below it, not closer to
it. The statement in Section~4.1.5 that the design resolves only shifts above
roughly $3.6\%$ therefore holds a fortiori, and nothing in the body requires
revision.

\subsection*{What controls the trace grade}

The resolution above is far coarser than three of the four trace-grade shifts, so
it cannot be what licenses them. Those rest instead on the repeatability of the
tap-based estimate within a cell, which is measured directly and is an order of
magnitude tighter.

five taps of each cell. Compare the $3.59\%$ resolution of the swept-sine test.}
\label{tab:lin-trace}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}

\midrule

\subsection*{Conclusion}

No dependence of $f_1$ on drive amplitude was detected across a factor of 2.2 in
drive. This is an absence of a detected effect and not a demonstration of
linearity: the design resolves shifts above roughly $3.6\%$ by a two-sigma
criterion, and above roughly $5.3\%$ formally, so an amplitude dependence smaller
than that would not have been found. The graded-series conclusions of Chapter~4
do not rest on this test. Tap amplitude across the graded series spans a factor
of $2.5$ by set mean, inside the range tested here, and the within-cell tap
scatter of Table~\ref{tab:lin-trace} bounds the combined effect of drive
variation and estimator noise at below $0.3\%$ at every trace cell.
